What gives the bulbar urethra its name and what is its blood supply?
column2: The bulbar urethra is surrounded by the corpus spongiosum's bulbar dilation just distal to the urogenital diaphragm; vascular supply is from the bulbar (bulbourethral) arteries off the internal pudendal artery.

column1: Where does the left ovarian vein drain, and where does the right drain?
column2: Left → left renal vein. Right → directly into the IVC (usually within 25 mm below the right renal vein ostium). The asymmetry underlies left-sided pelvic congestion and nutcracker susceptibility.

column1: What does the deep uterine vein divide laterally and why does it matter surgically?
column2: The DUV divides the lateral uterine aspect into a superior vascular zone (uterine artery, ureter) and an inferior nervous zone (inferior hypogastric plexus). Identifying it enables nerve-sparing radical hysterectomy and safer uterine transplantation.

column1: What is the female urethral continence mechanism and length?
column2: ~4 cm long; the striated rhabdosphincter is most concentrated in the mid-urethra at 54–66% of the length.

column1: What three components contribute to the urothelial barrier?
column2: E-cadherin, ZO-1, and uroplakin III. Loss of these underlies acute radiation cystitis and BPS/IC pathophysiology.

column1: What nerves form the inferior hypogastric plexus?
column2: Sympathetic (T11–L2 via hypogastric nerves) + parasympathetic (S2–S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) + somatic afferents.

column1: What is endarteritis obliterans and why does it matter to reconstructive surgery?
column2: Progressive obliterative vascular injury from radiation (endothelial death, fibrosis, chronic hypoxia). It makes the irradiated bed hypovascular, hypocellular, and hypoxic — grafts fail; well-vascularized flaps are preferred.

column1: What are the four pelvic venous escape points to the lower extremity?
column2: Inguinal (round ligament → vulva/groin), obturator (medial thigh), perineal (vulva/perineum), gluteal (greater sciatic foramen → posterior thigh/buttock, including intra/peri-neural sciatic varices).

column1: How many throws are needed for a secure square knot with monofilament suture?
column2: 6 throws (vs 4–5 for multifilament). Monofilament has lower interlayer friction and the knot can slip.

column1: Does wetting gloves with saline impair or improve knot security?
column2: Improves it. Pietschmann 2011: 14 wet vs 30 dry slippages (p < 0.05). Coleridge 2017: fluid media at worst neutral, often improves knot-holding capacity.

column1: What happens to knot failure load with petroleum-exposed sutures?
column2: It decreases. Muffly 2012: 116.7 N petroleum vs 123.8 N saline-soaked (p = 0.002). Petroleum reduces inter-strand friction inside the knot itself.

column1: What is the defining maneuver of the Heaney stitch?
column2: A transfixion suture-ligature with a double throw around the clamp — used for pelvic-pedicle control in vaginal and abdominal hysterectomy. Named for Noble Sproat Heaney.

column1: Why is bacitracin irrigation contraindicated per SHEA/IDSA 2022?
column2: Documented intraoperative anaphylactic shock cases; injectable bacitracin was withdrawn from the US market. Smack 1996 RCT also showed no infection benefit vs petrolatum and four allergic-contact-dermatitis cases in the bacitracin arm.

column1: Triclosan-coated sutures vs bacitracin-soaked for surgical-site infection?
column2: Triclosan-coated sutures (Vicryl Plus, PDS Plus, Monocryl Plus) are the CDC-endorsed (Category II) engineered alternative; bacitracin coating has only modest in vitro activity plus an anaphylaxis pathway and no clinical SSI benefit.

column1: What is the optimal initial-twist count for a surgeon's knot?
column2: 3–5 twists; benefit plateaus beyond 5.

column1: What is the friction-elastoplasticity framework for surgical knot strength (Johanns 2023)?
column2: Knot strength depends critically on inter-strand friction inside the knot; any agent that excessively reduces this friction (e.g., petroleum lubricants) compromises slippage resistance.

column1: First-line oral therapy for overactive bladder per AUA 2024?
column2: Behavioral therapy + beta-3 agonist (mirabegron or vibegron) or anticholinergic. Beta-3 agonists are preferred in the elderly to limit anticholinergic burden.

column1: When is desmopressin first-line and what is the key safety monitor?
column2: Nocturnal polyuria in patients with low risk of hyponatremia. Monitor serum sodium before initiation and periodically.

column1: Standard infection prophylaxis at AUS / IPP implantation?
column2: Vancomycin + gentamicin within 1 hour of incision, per AUA prosthetic-urinary-surgery best practice.

column1: What is the 2025 AUA/SUFU/AUGS first-choice for genitourinary syndrome of menopause?
column2: Low-dose vaginal estrogen (first-line). Alternatives include vaginal DHEA, ospemifene, and CO2 laser; consider survivorship context in breast-cancer survivors per NCCN.

column1: First-line imaging for urethral stricture?
column2: Retrograde urethrography (RUG); add VCUG to evaluate the posterior urethra and define distal extent.

column1: ICRP eye-lens dose limit per year?
column2: 20 mSv/year averaged over 5 years (revised down from the prior 150 mSv/year). The eye lens is the rate-limiting organ in high-volume endourology.

column1: FLASH UK reference DAP for PCNL?
column2: 24.1 Gy·cm² (fluoroscopy time 431 s) — the highest-dose urology procedure. High-volume centers achieve ~3× lower DAP than low-volume.

column1: Inverse-square law applied to fluoroscopy?
column2: Tripling distance from the X-ray source reduces scatter exposure 9-fold. Default to the image-intensifier side and prefer under-couch tube configurations.

column1: By how much does pulsed half-dose fluoroscopy reduce entrance skin dose?
column2: ~30% across all endourology; 33% specifically for PCNL (Canales 2016, p < 0.05). Combine with last-image hold and collimation.

column1: First-line imaging for suspected pelvic congestion syndrome in chronic pelvic pain?
column2: Transvaginal ultrasound with venous Doppler — ovarian vein > 7–8 mm, slow / retrograde flow, dilated (> 5 mm) pelvic veins. ~96% correlation with catheter venography.

column1: Gold standard for diagnosis of detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia?
column2: Multichannel urodynamics with simultaneous EMG, or video-urodynamics for anatomic localization. Essential in NLUTD evaluation.

column1: When is video-urodynamics preferred over standard UDS?
column2: When VUR, anatomic abnormality, or bladder-outlet obstruction is suspected — especially in neurogenic lower-urinary-tract dysfunction.

column1: What is the NIH-CPSI scale and what change is clinically meaningful?
column2: National Institutes of Health Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index — 0–43 scale measuring CP/CPPS severity. A 6-point change is the threshold for clinically meaningful improvement.

column1: What is the pathognomonic feature of pelvic congestion syndrome?
column2: Post-coital pain. Other features: dull aching pelvic pain worsened by prolonged standing or premenstrually; vulvar varicosities; predominantly premenopausal parous women.

column1: What proportion of chronic pelvic pain in women may be attributable to pelvic venous disorders?
column2: Up to ~30% — frequently underdiagnosed. ACOG considers the causation evidence insufficient, but the evidence-based endovascular treatment effect (Hansrani 2023 RCT) is real.

column1: What are the SVP classification zones for pelvic venous disorders?
column2: Z1 = left renal vein. Z2 = gonadal + internal iliac veins + pelvic plexuses. Z3 = pelvic-origin extra-pelvic transitional veins (escape points). Z4 = lower-extremity veins (classified per CEAP).

column1: What is the prevalence of Hunner lesions in BPS/IC?
column2: ~5–10% — a distinct phenotype with different treatment responses (Hunner-lesion–specific therapies including fulguration / triamcinolone injection).

column1: Most common contributors to chronic pelvic pain across all patients?
column2: Irritable bowel syndrome, bladder pain syndrome / interstitial cystitis, myofascial pelvic-floor dysfunction, and (in women) endometriosis.

column1: 12-year hazard ratio for urethral stricture after prostate radiotherapy?
column2: > 6-fold vs untreated (Unger 2024 JAMA Oncology). Radiation-cystitis risk is > 130-fold higher in the same series.

column1: Most common location of post-radiation urethral stricture?
column2: Bulbomembranous urethra (~83% in meta-analysis). Endoscopic management has limited durability in the irradiated field.

column1: Pooled urethroplasty success rate for radiation-induced urethral stenosis?
column2: 80% (95% CI 74–86%) — Sapienza 2021 meta-analysis (n = 256). Independent of RT modality or urethroplasty technique; ~1 in 5 patients develops de novo stress urinary incontinence.

column1: AUS social-continence rate in irradiated patients?
column2: ~87–95% — comparable to non-radiated cohorts. However, device durability is reduced: HR 3.3 for cuff removal, HR 7.6 for erosion/infection of replacement devices.

column1: Recommended interval before AUS implantation after pelvic radiation?
column2: > 1.5–2 years post-RT may be associated with lower cuff-removal rates (Lee 2025 exploratory). Adjuvant RT independently predicts all-cause failure (HR 4.32).

column1: What is the first-line endovascular treatment for primary pelvic vein reflux causing PCS?
column2: Ovarian / pelvic vein embolization with coils, plugs, or sclerosant. Technical success ~100%. Hansrani 2023 RCT showed SF-MPQ pain 2 vs 9 (p = 0.016) at 12 months.

column1: Treatment order when reflux and obstruction coexist in PeVD?
column2: Treat the obstruction first (iliac stent for May-Thurner, balloon angioplasty for nutcracker), then assess for ongoing reflux requiring embolization.

column1: What is the 2026 Emory POTS / orthostatic-intolerance association with PeVD?
column2: 83% prevalence of PeVD among POTS/OI patients (Spencer 2026). After iliac stenting: 44% complete resolution of orthostatic symptoms; 71% significant clinical improvement at 1 year. Reframes some POTS as compensatory tachycardia from venous obstruction.

column1: Most common type of female urinary fistula in developed countries?
column2: Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF), most often iatrogenic following hysterectomy. Globally, obstetric VVF predominates.

column1: First-line workup for suspected vesicovaginal fistula?
column2: Cystoscopy + vaginal exam + cystography or CT cystogram. Add double-dye (tampon) test for occult or ureteral involvement.

column1: Bulbar urethral stricture EPA success rate?
column2: 93.8% pooled in the SIU/ICUD consultation (Wessells/Webster 2014; 1,234 patients). Gold standard for short (≤ 2 cm) bulbar strictures.

column1: Posterior urethroplasty success after PFUI in Koraitim's series?
column2: 90–98% over 27 years. Standard pathway: suprapubic-cystostomy-first → delayed anastomotic urethroplasty at 3 months → perineal approach.

column1: Buccal mucosa graft urethroplasty success in post-radiation strictures?
column2: Long-term success 70–100% in specialized series; pooled 80% per Sapienza 2021 meta. Counsel re: ~10–20% de novo SUI risk.

column1: First-line management of recurrent bladder-neck contracture after radical prostatectomy?
column2: Endoscopic incision (DVIU) for first attempts; transition to reconstructive options (Y-V plasty, subtrigonal BMG inlay, robotic bladder-flap posterior urethroplasty) after ≥ 2 failed endoscopic treatments.

column1: Preferred tissue for reconstruction in an irradiated field?
column2: Well-vascularized FLAP (gracilis, omental, Singapore, VRAM, Martius) — the irradiated bed cannot reliably support graft take. Graft choice is salvageable only with careful bed preparation and small-defect application.

column1: Most common long-term stomal complication after urinary diversion?
column2: Parastomal hernia. Repair options: Sugarbaker, keyhole, sandwich, or 3-D mesh techniques; prophylactic mesh at construction is increasingly favored.

column1: Indication for the Mitrofanoff procedure?
column2: Continent catheterizable channel for clean intermittent catheterization in neurogenic bladder. Appendix-based (true Mitrofanoff) or detubularized bowel via Yang-Monti.

column1: What defines "social continence" after AUS?
column2: 0–1 pads per day. Anatomic / "complete" continence = 0 pads. The latter is the historical AUS endpoint.

column1: What is the primary indication for hyperbaric oxygen therapy in reconstructive urology?
column2: Hemorrhagic radiation cystitis (RICH-ART RCT — long-term symptom and QoL improvement at 5 yr). Also preconditioning irradiated tissue before reconstruction; Fournier's-gangrene adjunct; chronic radiation-induced fistulas.

column1: Indications for tissue interposition flap in fistula repair?
column2: Recurrent, radiated, or complex fistulas. Standard options: Martius (vulvar/perineal), gracilis (perineal/trans-thigh), omental (transabdominal), peritoneal flap (robotic transabdominal).

column1: First-line management of hypospadias-related urethrocutaneous fistula?
column2: Wait ≥ 6 months from index surgery for tissue maturation, then layered closure with non-overlapping suture lines + dartos / scrotal / Martius interposition as needed.

column1: Indication for transcorporal AUS cuff placement?
column2: Severely compromised urethra after prior procedures, radiation, or thin urethra at risk of erosion. Improves durability vs standard cuff placement (3.5 cm cuff associated with HR 8.62 failure risk).

column1: Bladder-neck closure (BNC) primary indication?
column2: Devastated urethra after chronic catheterization or failed bladder-neck procedures, requiring permanent continent diversion via Mitrofanoff or similar channel.

column1: Complication rate of salvage cystectomy after pelvic radiation?
column2: Overall 75% complication rate; Clavien ≥ 3 in 30%; mortality 2.9–6.1%. 3-fold higher odds of rectal injury (OR 3.17). Orthotopic neobladder feasible in highly selected patients; 86% receive incontinent diversion.

column1: Radiation cystitis management ladder?
column2: Conservative (hydration, anticholinergics) → intravesical (hyaluronic acid, alum, formalin) → endoscopic cautery of telangiectasia → HBOT (30–40 sessions, 2.0–2.5 ATA) → urinary diversion ± cystectomy.

column1: 3-piece IPP vs malleable prosthesis selection?
column2: IPP — preserved dexterity, longer life expectancy, partner involvement, more natural concealment. Malleable — limited dexterity, simpler surgery, less reservoir-space concern (prior renal transplant, ARP scarred pelvis), single-stage availability.

column1: Modern first-line vaginoplasty technique for gender-affirming surgery?
column2: Penile-inversion vaginoplasty (Selvaggi/Hoebeke modernized 2009): cranially pedicled U-flaps + V-Y advancement + 90° medial rotation + fat-pad relocation. Most common feminizing genital surgery.

column1: Indication for intestinal vaginoplasty (sigmoid / robotic peritoneal)?
column2: Failed primary PIV with depth loss; persistent mucus-secreting depth desired (14–17.6 cm); penile skin insufficient for primary.

column1: Most common urethral complication after feminizing vaginoplasty?
column2: Meatal stenosis (Dreher 2018: 14.4%, range 4–40%). Stepwise management: office dilation → dorsal meatotomy → Y-V meatoplasty.

column1: Transmasculine penile prosthesis explantation rate?
column2: Overall 20.8% in Pigot 2019 (n = 206, mean 11.5-yr follow-up). Drops to 11.5% with modern Hoebeke V-Y scrotoplasty technique. Smoking is the dominant modifiable risk factor.

column1: Best-evidence phalloplasty flap for sensate transmasculine reconstruction?
column2: Radial forearm free flap (RFFF) — gold standard for sensation + urethral lengthening + functional penetration. Donor-site morbidity is the main tradeoff.

column1: Who described the Heaney stitch, where, and when?
column2: Noble Sproat Heaney (1880–1955), Chicago. His vaginal hysterectomy technique codified the modern approach to pelvic pedicle control; the eponymous needle holder and retractor share his name.

column1: Who developed the Mitrofanoff principle and when?
column2: Paul Mitrofanoff, 1980, France — initial description in pediatric neurogenic bladder. Appendix-based continent catheterizable channel for clean intermittent catheterization.

column1: Why does Sushruta matter to reconstructive urology?
column2: Ancient Indian surgeon (~6th century BC). The Sushruta Samhita describes reed catheters for urethral dilation — foundational text in the urology lineage that extends through Boari, Mitrofanoff, and modern urethroplasty.

column1: Who is the eponym behind the Boari flap?
column2: Alessandro Boari (early 1900s, Italy). Bladder-flap ureteroplasty for distal ureteral defects too long for psoas hitch alone.

column1: AUA 2022 IC/BPS guideline first-line treatment?
column2: Patient education + behavioral modifications + stress management; OTC analgesics; pain-management referral. The 2022 update replaced the tiered first-to-sixth-line structure with categorical management.

column1: AUA 2023 Urethral Stricture Disease Guideline — preferred bulbar stricture < 2 cm management?
column2: Excision and primary anastomosis (EPA) — gold standard with ~95% success in short strictures.

column1: CDC 2017 SSI Prevention — application of antimicrobial agents to the surgical incision?
column2: Recommended AGAINST (Category IB). Consider triclosan-coated sutures (Category II) as the engineered alternative for antimicrobial benefit at the suture line.

column1: WPATH SOC8 — surgical eligibility prerequisite for gender-affirming surgery?
column2: Persistent gender dysphoria + capacity to consent + age of majority (with informed-consent process). SOC8 no longer requires a letter from a secondary mental-health provider for adults.

column1: SVS/AVF/AVLS 2023 varicose-veins guideline — pelvic-origin lower-extremity varicosities?
column2: Bottom-up approach: treat the escape points and extra-pelvic varicosities first (foam sclerotherapy or ligation); escalate to ovarian-vein embolization or iliac-vein stenting only for refractory or pelvic-symptom development.

column1: EAU 2024 priapism — early malleable penile prosthesis placement criteria?
column2: 48-h irreversibility threshold (priapism > 48 h ≈ 100% necrotic smooth muscle on biopsy). MRI-guided patient selection (Ralph 2010 100% sensitivity). Early MPP: 0% cylinder shortening vs 40.5% delayed (Barham 2023).

column1: AAST grade IV renal injury definition?
column2: Pelvicalyceal or ureteropelvic junction laceration with extravasation; OR main renal vessel laceration with contained hematoma. Grade V = shattered kidney or avulsed renal pedicle.

column1: What percentage of pelvic fractures result in posterior urethral injury?
column2: 5–10%. Suprapubic-cystostomy first; delayed anastomotic urethroplasty at 3 months is the Koraitim-pathway gold standard.

column1: Management of testicular torsion presenting within 6 hours?
column2: Manual detorsion (lateral rotation, "open the book") at bedside as a bridge → emergent surgical exploration with bilateral orchiopexy. Salvage 90–100% if < 6 h, < 50% if > 12 h.

column1: Diagnostic cavernosal blood gas for ischemic priapism?
column2: pO2 < 30 mmHg, pCO2 > 60 mmHg, pH < 7.25. Non-ischemic priapism shows arterial values (often "high-flow" after pelvic trauma).

column1: Brant–Lue T-shunt 9-step approach?
column2: Lateral glans entry at the 2 and 10 o'clock positions; No. 10 blade incision into the distal corpus; 90° rotation of the blade within the corpus; Foley protection of the urethra. Compatible with the Burnett Snake maneuver.

column1: Intraperitoneal vs extraperitoneal bladder rupture — management?
column2: Intraperitoneal: surgical exploration + multilayer closure. Extraperitoneal: Foley catheter drainage and observation (most heal); operate if concomitant indications (bladder-neck involvement, pelvic-fracture fixation in the field, ongoing extravasation).

column1: Iatrogenic ureteral injury management by location — lower 1/3?
column2: Ureteroneocystostomy ± psoas hitch ± Boari flap by defect length. Goal: tension-free, refluxing or non-refluxing reimplant. Long defects → ileal interposition.

column1: Penile fracture definitive management?
column2: Same-day operative exploration + tunica albuginea repair via subcoronal degloving or local incision. Corporography rarely needed when clinical suspicion is strong (audible "pop," immediate detumescence, palpable defect).

column1: Most concerning sign of Fournier's gangrene?
column2: Pain out of proportion to exam + crepitus + LRINEC score ≥ 6 → emergent surgical debridement to viable bleeding tissue. Mortality 7–9% in modern series.

column1: Definitive reconstruction after Fournier's wound stabilization?
column2: Scrotal defects: STSG for moderate loss; perineal flaps (Singapore, gracilis, anteromedial-thigh perforator) for large defects. Testicular pouch in medial thigh if scrotal loss complete; staged neoscrotum reconstruction.

column1: First-line endourologic management of female stress urinary incontinence?
column2: Pelvic floor PT + lifestyle. Surgical first-line: mid-urethral sling (retropubic or transobturator); autologous fascial sling for selected (mesh aversion, recurrence, complicated cases). Bulking (PAHG / Bulkamid) for low-fixed-pressure / mild SUI.

column1: Indications for SNM vs Botox in refractory OAB after failed combination therapy?
column2: SNM — reversible, also treats DUA / non-obstructive retention and fecal incontinence; lead-revision rate ~15%. Botox — episodic re-treatments at 6–12 mo, CIC need 5–10%, fewer device-related issues. Patient preference drives choice.

column1: AUA 2024 BPH treatment ladder?
column2: Lifestyle/observation → α-blocker / 5-ARI / PDE5i → combination → MIST (UroLift, Rezum, iTind, TIPD, PAE) → surgical (TURP, HoLEP/ThuLEP/AquaBeam aquablation, simple prostatectomy for very large gland).

column1: Hinman syndrome — clinical hallmark?
column2: Non-neurogenic neurogenic bladder. Dysfunctional voiding (learned external-sphincter co-contraction during voiding) in the absence of neurologic lesion; often pediatric. Treatment: behavioral retraining, biofeedback, α-blockers; surgical only for refractory secondary upper-tract injury.

column1: Most common cause of female urethral diverticulum?
column2: Recurrent periurethral gland infection / obstruction → fluctuant midline cystic mass communicating with the urethra. Presents with the "3 D's": dysuria, dyspareunia, post-void dribbling.

column1: Standard surgical treatment of female urethral diverticulum?
column2: Transvaginal diverticulectomy with multilayer non-overlapping closure (urethra → periurethral fascia → vaginal wall). Consider concomitant pubovaginal sling if pre-op SUI documented.

column1: AUA 2022 recurrent UTI guideline — first-line for postmenopausal women?
column2: Vaginal estrogen + lifestyle/behavioral modification + targeted prophylactic strategy (cranberry, methenamine, low-dose daily antibiotic prophylaxis, post-coital prophylaxis, vaccines).

column1: Singapore flap (pudendal thigh fasciocutaneous flap) — primary indication?
column2: Vaginal reconstruction; posterior urethral defects in heavily scarred perineum (Tzarnas 1994 first urologic application). Wong-Wee 1989 original anatomic description.

column1: Yang-Monti principle?
column2: Detubularized ileum reconfigured perpendicular over a wire → retubularized as a narrow catheterizable channel. Used when appendix is unavailable for Mitrofanoff or for substitute ureter when bowel interposition is needed.

column1: AUS cuff size most associated with increased failure?
column2: 3.5 cm cuff (HR 8.62 for failure, McGeady 2014). Used in compromised / narrowed urethras after multiple prior procedures.

column1: Pelvic-floor PT effect on chronic pelvic pain?
column2: SMD -1.69 for short-term pain in women (high-certainty evidence); recommended by ACOG, AUA, EAU. Also effective in CP/CPPS in men.

column1: Vesico-uterine fistula management?
column2: Small/early: drainage ± GnRH-agonist amenorrhea (Józwik I). Persistent: delayed (≥ 3 mo) repair, uterine-sparing in reproductive-age patients.

column1: Posterior urethral distraction defect (PFUI) after suprapubic cystostomy — timing of definitive repair?
column2: Delayed anastomotic urethroplasty at 3 months — allows scar maturation, hematoma resorption, and full extent of stricture to declare. Earlier repair compromises planning.

column1: Augmentation cystoplasty long-term surveillance?
column2: Annual urinalysis + BMP (electrolyte, acidosis); annual B12 if ileal segment used; cystoscopy after 10 years (lifetime cancer risk ~1.5%, often signet-ring adenocarcinoma at the augment-bladder anastomosis).

column1: PCNL position and operator radiation dose?
column2: Prone is highest operator exposure. Supine PCNL reduces operator dose meaningfully and allows easier anesthetic management. Volume itself reduces dose: > 50 cases/yr ≈ 3× lower DAP than low-volume centers.

column1: Penile-Doppler ultrasound criteria for arterial sufficiency?
column2: PSV > 30 cm/s (some series 35); EDV < 5 cm/s; RI > 0.85 → normal arterial inflow. Arteriogenic ED: low PSV. Venogenic ED: high EDV, low RI with normal PSV.

column1: Sengezer 2004 fibula phalloplasty — defining feature?
column2: First sensate osteocutaneous free fibula flap for transmasculine reconstruction (n = 18 patients). Built-in rigidity from the fibular bone allows penetration without separate prosthesis.

column1: LRINEC score threshold for emergent operative exploration?
column2: LRINEC ≥ 6 strongly suggests necrotizing fasciitis / Fournier's; ≥ 8 is high-probability. Composed of CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose. Do not delay surgery for imaging if clinical suspicion is high.

column1: SUI prevalence after vesicovaginal fistula repair?
column2: Up to 52% develop post-repair SUI — counsel preoperatively; autologous pubovaginal sling is preferred for repair if concomitant or anticipated.

column1: First-line for ureterovaginal fistula?
column2: Retrograde or antegrade stenting (62% definitive when placed > 72 h). If failed, redo ureteroneocystostomy, ureteroureterostomy, Boari + psoas hitch, or omental wrap by defect length and patient candidacy.

column1: Indications for orthotopic neobladder after pelvic radiation?
column2: Feasible only in highly selected patients with adequate continence mechanism + tolerant bowel for ileal segment + no urethral involvement + motivated for self-catheterization rescue. 86% of irradiated patients in series ultimately receive incontinent diversion.

column1: First-line for urethrovaginal fistula?
column2: Transvaginal layered repair (90–100% success). Add Martius flap for tissue deficit, recurrence, or radiation. Counsel re: post-repair SUI risk.

column1: What is the most common urethral complication of brachytherapy?
column2: Bulbomembranous urethral stricture. Brachytherapy rate 18.4% vs 5.2% for EBRT alone in ASCENDE-RT trial.

column1: Best graft donor site for urethral reconstruction overall?
column2: Buccal mucosa graft — hairless, robust, easy harvest, 70–100% long-term success in non-radiated bulbar urethroplasty. Lingual and labial mucosa are second-line; harvest morbidity tradeoffs differ.

column1: AUS double-cuff implantation — when?
column2: Severe SUI refractory to single cuff. Maurer 2019: no significant difference in continence or complication rates between RT and non-RT patients for double-cuff specifically.

column1: Indication for fecal diversion in fistula management?
column2: Adjunct or definitive for complex / radiated rectourinary or rectovaginal fistulas. Diverting stoma independently predicts repair success (Corte OR 3.5).

column1: What is the AUA-recommended PSA-monitoring interval after radical prostatectomy?
column2: Every 6–12 months for the first 5 years, then annually; ultrasensitive PSA enables earlier detection of biochemical recurrence but does not change current AUA threshold (0.2 ng/mL with subsequent confirmatory rise).

column1: Bulkamid (PAHG) — primary indication?
column2: Female stress urinary incontinence — durable continence improvement 50–65% at 1–2 years. Office-based, repeatable, useful in patients averse to mesh sling.

column1: What classifies female stress urinary incontinence as "intrinsic sphincter deficiency" (ISD)?
column2: MUCP < 20 cm H2O OR VLPP < 60 cm H2O on urodynamics. ISD predicts inferior response to retropubic sling vs autologous fascial sling or AUS.

column1: Sacrocolpopexy success rate?
column2: Long-term anatomic success > 90% for apical support; functional outcomes (sexual function, urinary symptoms) less consistently superior to native-tissue repair. Mesh-related complication rate 2–5% over follow-up.

column1: What flap is preferred for posterior urethral reconstruction after recto-urethral fistula failure?
column2: Gracilis muscle interposition flap (Singapore, omentum as alternatives) — vascular bulk to separate the rectum from urethra. Pelvic radiation predicts persistent incontinence even after successful gracilis repair (Raup 2016).

column1: Indications for ileal ureter substitution?
column2: Long (> 5 cm) ureteral defect not reconstructable with Boari + psoas hitch. Contraindications: small bowel disease, baseline acidosis, severe renal impairment (relative — concentrating defect amplifies absorption).

column1: Most common cause of upper-tract deterioration in neurogenic bladder?
column2: Sustained high detrusor leak-point pressure (LPP > 40 cm H2O = McGuire threshold) → upper-tract dilation and renal compromise. Annual UDS or compliance evaluation drives management changes.

column1: McGuire's leak-point pressure threshold predicting upper-tract injury?
column2: > 40 cm H2O detrusor leak-point pressure in spinal-cord injury / myelomeningocele. Indicates inadequate compliance; intervention (anticholinergic escalation, Botox, augmentation cystoplasty) is indicated to preserve renal function.

column1: Definition of autonomic dysreflexia?
column2: Acute uncontrolled sympathetic discharge in patients with SCI above T6 in response to noxious stimulus below the lesion. SBP rise > 20 mmHg above baseline. Immediate treatment: sit patient up, identify and remove trigger (catheterize for retention is #1), nifedipine SL if persistent.

column1: Why is sacral neuromodulation contraindicated in dementia and severe neurogenic bladder?
column2: Patient cannot reliably report sensory/efficacy feedback; settings require iterative titration. Also avoid in pregnancy (potential fetal nerve stimulation). Relative contraindication in severe SCI where reflex bladder may not respond.

column1: Posterior tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS) — typical treatment cadence?
column2: Weekly 30-min sessions × 12 weeks induction, then monthly maintenance. Comparable continence response to anticholinergic monotherapy in OAB; well-tolerated alternative for medication-intolerant patients.

column1: Female pelvic organ prolapse — POP-Q stages?
column2: Stage 0: no descent. Stage 1: leading edge > 1 cm above hymen. Stage 2: within 1 cm of hymen. Stage 3: > 1 cm below hymen but not procidentia. Stage 4: complete eversion / procidentia.

column1: Indication for colpocleisis (obliterative prolapse repair)?
column2: Elderly, sexually inactive patient with advanced POP, often with comorbidities limiting tolerance for major reconstruction. Le Fort partial or total colpocleisis. ~90% anatomic success; counsel re: irreversible loss of vaginal canal.

column1: Mesh-augmented vs native-tissue anterior vaginal repair?
column2: Transvaginal mesh removed from US market (FDA 2019) for anterior compartment. Sacrocolpopexy with mesh remains supported for apical prolapse. Native-tissue repair preferred for primary anterior repair; mesh reserved for highly selected recurrent cases.

column1: Indications for tibial nerve stimulation (eCoin / Axonics)?
column2: Refractory OAB / urge incontinence. Implantable PTNS devices (eCoin tibial nerve, Axonics rechargeable) offer office-based delivery without weekly visits. Comparable outcomes to SNM for OAB but no DUA / fecal incontinence indication.

column1: Primary mechanism of action of mirabegron / vibegron?
column2: Beta-3 adrenergic agonism → detrusor relaxation during storage phase. Lower anticholinergic burden than antimuscarinics. Mirabegron monitor BP (small SBP increase); vibegron has cleaner CV profile.

column1: Highest-yield indication for HBOT in late radiation injury?
column2: Hemorrhagic radiation cystitis (RICH-ART 2019, 5-yr follow-up 2025) — improved macroscopic bladder appearance, symptom burden, QoL. Also chronic radiation-induced fistula (low-certainty Cochrane). 30–40 sessions at 2.0–2.5 ATA; 2.5 ATA may be superior for hematuria.
